### C-R9-01
**Claim:** Jer 46–51 especially fulfills Jeremiah’s commission as a prophet regarding the nations; Hananiah’s words (28:8) would be an apt epigraph—earlier prophets prophesied about many countries and big kingdoms concerning battle, dire fortune, and epidemic.
**Quote:** “Many Western readers might prefer the prophetic scrolls without the prophecies about God bringing disaster to other nations, but Jer 46–51 especially reflects Jeremiah’s fulfillment of his commission to be a prophet regarding the nations. His words to Hananiah would make an appropriate epigraph to the chapters: The prophets who were before me and before you from of old, they prophesied regarding many countries and concerning big kingdoms, about battle and about dire fortune and about epidemic (28:8).”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 3–4; Jer 46–51; 28:8
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R9-02
**Claim:** Prophecies about other nations are integral to prophecy in Israel’s world—among the oldest prophetic material—assuring a people that their god would protect them and put down enemies; Yahweh takes prophecy (like priesthood and kingship) from Israel’s world and adapts it. Prophecies about Israel grow out of speaking about the nations, not the reverse.
**Quote:** “Prophecies about other nations are integral to prophecy in Israel’s world; a major function of prophecy was to assure a people and its monarch that their god was going to protect them, give them victory, and put down their enemies. Such prophecies may be the oldest prophetic material that there is. … the prophecies about Israel have their origin in a way of thinking and speaking about the nations, not the opposite. With prophecy, as with priesthood and kingship, Yahweh takes something from Israel’s world and adapts it to his purpose.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 5–6
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R9-03
**Claim:** Different prophetic scrolls deploy OAN differently: Amos softens Ephraim; Isa 1–39 underscores neither relying on nor fearing nations and moves from Judah (1–12) to world horizon (24–27); Ezekiel transitions from confrontation (1–24) to promise (33–48).
**Quote:** “In Amos, prophecies about other nations soften up Ephraim for the prophet’s confrontation of Ephraim itself. In Isa 1–39, they underscore a concern that Judah should neither rely on other nations nor be afraid of them, and they form part of a movement from Judah itself being the focus (Isa 1–12) to the world becoming the horizon (Isa 24–27). In Ezekiel, they form part of the transition from confrontation and threat (Ezek 1–24) to promise and hope (Ezek 33–48).”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 5–6
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R9-05
**Claim:** MT places OAN almost at the end (after 45; with post-587 material in 37–45 and 52); LXX places them in the middle after Jer 25. Neither order is known to be more original; both make sense. In LXX they spell out 25:1–13 and contribute to an alternation of confrontation/promise; in MT they follow 45, do not interrupt Judah material (26–45 follows 25), close with a worldwide horizon, and transition from bad news to good news for Judah via putting down the agent of destruction.
**Quote:** “In Jeremiah, whereas this collection of prophecies about the nations appears almost at the end of the scroll in MT, in LXX it appears in the middle, following on Jer 25. We do not know whether either order is more original or whether they represent ways in which different curators assembled Jeremianic material; either position makes sense. In LXX Jeremiah, they spell out the declaration of calamity for the nations in 25:1–13. … In MT Jeremiah, they instead follow on Jer 45 and come with other material focusing on events after 587, in Jer 37–45 and 52. On one hand, they thus do not interrupt Jeremiah’s material relating to Judah, as Jer 26–45 follows on Jer 25. And on the other, they make the Jeremiah scroll (almost) close with a worldwide horizon and, in the promise about putting down the great agent of destruction and exile, make for a transition from bad news for Judah to good news for Judah after the false dawn in Jer 30–33.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 10–11; Jer 46–51 / LXX 26–31
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R9-06
**Claim:** OAN focus more on the fact of calamity than on reasons; compared with Rom 1–3 the combination (Israel + world under judgment) is the same but order is reverse, and Romans attends as much to reasons as to trouble.
**Quote:** “The chapters do not give much consideration to reasons for the trouble that comes to the different peoples. The focus is more on the fact of calamity than on the reasons. The point about the chapters thus compares and contrasts with the argument of Rom 1–3. … the combination is the same, but the order is the reverse. And here, the focus lies on the fact of trouble coming rather than the reasons for it, whereas Romans pays as much attention to the reasons as to the trouble itself.”

### C-R9-07
**Claim:** Unlike Judah oracles, OAN rarely refer to Yahweh’s wrath/anger (only 49:37; 51:45); accusation is “extremely laconic,” highlighting that the really guilty party is Yahweh’s own people. Jeremiah does speak of redress (46:10; 50:15, 28; 51:6, 11, 36), shaming false confidence (46:24; 48:1, 7, 29; 49:4, 16), acting against expansionist ambitions (46:8), and vindicating Yahweh as only real God (48:7). For imperial powers, focus is grandeur/confidence; Babylon is agent in 46–49 and victim in 50–51.
**Quote:** “Unlike the messages that confront Judah, these chapters refer little to Yahweh’s wrath or anger (49:37; 51:45), and ‘the use of accusation and indictment’ is ‘extremely laconic.’ This shortfall further highlights how the really guilty party in Jeremiah is the people of Yahweh. … With some irony, Babylon is the agent of calamity in Jer 46–49 and the victim of it in Jer 50–51. But the logic of including other powers—Judah’s neighbors and the representative eastern ones—is simply that they become illustrations of Yahweh’s being sovereign in the entire world of nations.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 14–15
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R9-08
**Claim:** Distant-peoples oracles (49:23–39) give no reason for calamity, raising whether “prophecies of judgment” is right language; shared store of phrases recurs within 46–51 and across prophets. Dating concentrations (46:2; 47:1; 49:34; 51:59) suggest concrete historical contexts; Jer 27 envoys offer one setting. Unlike Amos-style neighbor oracles, almost no punishment-for-harm-to-Israel motif except Ammon and at points Babylon—none in Egypt, Moab, Edom, Damascus, Kedar, Elam.
**Quote:** “Some of the messages concern distant peoples that do not impinge on Judah (49:23–39), and these messages give no reason for the calamity that is coming on their subjects, which raises the question whether ‘prophecies of judgment’ is at all the right way to describe the messages about other nations. … There is a marked concentration of the dating of messages in Jer 46–51 (46:2; 47:1; 49:34; 51:59)…. Like the messages about other peoples in Amos, the messages in Jer 46–51 include virtually no indications that the nations are being punished for what they have done to Israel. While this motif does appear in the message about Ammon and at one or two points in the gargantuan message about Babylon, it features not at all in the messages about Egypt, Moab, Edom, Damascus, Kedar, and Elam.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 14–16
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R9-09
**Claim:** “Oracles against the Nations” is misleading: nations receive promises (46:26; 48:47; 49:6; 49:39) and sympathy (47; 48); restoration, not judgment, is God’s last word. Jeremiah was commissioned “to build and to plant” as well as pull down (1:10), for them as well as Judah. No exhortation to repentance (unlike Judah); messages addressed to Judah, not the nations; Jonah-like implied challenge may still stand.
**Quote:** “Further, the prophecies are not just about putting other nations down, and a title such as ‘Oracles against the Nations’ also gives a misleading impression. The nations are the recipients of promises (46:26; 48:47; 49:6; 49:39) and of sympathy (47; 48). And the promises of restoration for different nations rule out chauvinism. Restoration, not judgment, is God’s last word. Jeremiah was, after all, commissioned ‘to build and to plant’ as well as ‘to pull up and pull down’ (1:10), for them as well as for Judah. For them, unlike Judah, there is no exhortation to repentance or promise that judgment can be escaped. But that characteristic reminds us that these messages were not addressed to the nations themselves but to Judah…”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 16–17
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R9-10
**Claim:** OAN are not standardized—vary in length, complexity, unity, chronology, rationale, relation to Judah. Typical motifs: army defeat, calamity from the north, Yahweh’s day, shame. MT and LXX order of individual messages differ: LXX puts Babylon mid-sequence; MT puts Babylon last. LXX order looks random; MT has geographical-theological logic: Egypt/Philistia (SW) → Moab/Ammon/Edom (E neighbors) → Damascus/Kedar/Hazor/Elam (distant, lordship over all) → Babylon (most important; agent of downfall). First half: Babylon furthers Yahweh’s designs; second half: Babylon falls like the rest.
**Quote:** “Typically, they describe an army experiencing defeat, a calamity arriving from the north; it comes as Yahweh’s day, and the result is shame. … LXX thus has the message about Babylon in the middle of the sequence while MT has it at the end…. LXX’s order looks random, whereas there is a broad geographical and theological logic about MT’s. It begins from the south and west, with Egypt … and Philistia; goes on to Judah’s neighbors to the east … Moab … Ammon and Edom; moves to Damascus, Kedar, Hazor, and Elam … finally comes to Babylon…. The MT sequence means that in the first half ‘Babylonian imperial predation still furthers Yahweh’s own imperial designs’ while in the second half ‘the Babylonian beast … goes to the ground as its Yahwistic master treats it to the same fate as the rest of the world’…”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 18–33
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R9-11
**Claim:** Part 5A (46:1–28) structure: one-line intro (v. 1); two poems (2–12 Carchemish eve; 13–24 Nebuchadrezzar invasion); two footnotes (25–26 Egypt restored after Nebuchadrezzar; 27–28 promise to Israel of scatter then return). Little rationale for Egypt’s calamity; most likely self-confident, arrogant imperial pretensions (vv. 7–8, 12). Temple-court hearers in Jehoiakim’s day: folly of relying on Egypt; after 587: hope of own freedom/restoration.
**Quote:** “Part 5 begins with a one-line introduction to the set of passages about the other nations. … Like other messages about the nations, the unit offers little insight on the rationale for bringing calamity on Egypt. … Most likely, Yahweh attacks it because of its self-confident, arrogant pretensions (cf. vv. 7–8, 12). It had imperial designs, and Yahweh is inclined to be against empires. Hearing such a message proclaimed in the temple courts, Judahites in Jehoiakim’s day might be given food for thought about the folly of treating Egypt as a potential resource and support. After 587, Judahites might be encouraged about the prospects of their own eventual freedom, restoration, and independence.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 40–69; Jer 46:1–28
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R9-12
**Claim:** 46:1–12: each half moves from army preparation (3–4, 7–9) to aftermath of hopeless defeat (5–6, 10–12)—no battle description; more point if delivered before Carchemish. Poetry parallels opening Judah calamity visions; ironic readiness; terror all around as for Judah (6:25 etc.). Carchemish 605 initiated Babylon’s era; Egypt was bigger—Judah not stupid to see it as ally; history unpredictable because some days Yahweh decides are his day (v. 10).
**Quote:** “Neither half describes the battle itself; the message focuses on the preparation and the aftermath. There would be more point to the message if it preceded the event rather than describing it afterward…. The Egyptian army is making ready for battle like the northern army making ready to invade Judah…. But it is now operating not against Judah but against Egypt…. Modern readers might see the victory as predictable and inevitable. It wasn’t. Egypt was a bigger nation than Babylon…. The message assumes that there are sometimes occasions that Yahweh decides to treat as his occasion; some days he decides to treat as his day (v. 10). It is one consideration that makes history unpredictable.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 220–266; Jer 46:1–12
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R9-14
**Claim:** 46:3–6: identity of commissioning voice and whose warriors flee is initially elusive (Babylon or Egypt)—pro-Egyptian Jehoiakim policy vs. those glad Neco killed Josiah; poetry’s elusiveness forces continued listening. Ridicule is Jeremiah’s “chief weapon.” “North” is both legendary home of consuming forces (cf. 1:14) and literal Euphrates. Mockery of Egypt also disgraces Judahites counting on Egypt vs. Babylon.
**Quote:** “Jeremiah does not indicate who is commissioning the warriors—he or their commander or Yahweh. … Nor does Jeremiah make clear whose warriors are being commissioned or whose warriors are running for their lives—Babylon’s or Egypt’s. … So the message works with the elusiveness that often characterizes prophecy expressed in poetry. … In this chapter, ridicule is Jeremiah’s ‘chief weapon.’ … The legendary north stands not merely for a place in terms of literal geography … but for the home of fabled forces that could consume anyone’s world (cf. 1:14). … The mockery of Egypt would not only imply Egypt’s disgrace; it would also disgrace people in Judah who were counting on Egypt as a counterbalance to Babylon.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 273–304; Jer 46:3–6
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

The message adds to the first one the fact that Yahweh is capable of defeating the gods that allegedly protected a nation such as Egypt…. ### C-R9-17
**Claim:** 46:25–26: prose summary—Yahweh attends to Amon of Thebes, Pharaoh, Egypt, gods, kings, those who rely on him; gives them to Nebuchadrezzar; but afterward Egypt will dwell as in former days. Complements Memphis/Apis with Thebes/Amon. Nebuchadrezzar first named in poetry-unit messages only in prose form. Restoration fits 1:10 commission; freedom to be itself without being great empire again (cf. Ezek 29:13–16). Stupid to rely on Pharaoh—Judahite admin pre-587; Johanan’s group later.
**Quote:** “The unexpected feature of the message is the closing promise, though it fits Jeremiah’s original commission. As a prophet concerning nations and kingdoms, Jeremiah was commissioned to build and plant as well as pull down and pull up. … Yahweh’s worldwide lordship makes it not surprising to find a promise to restore Egypt. The message does not spell out the promise’s cash value in the variegated way that Isa 19:18–25 does. It does suggest a freedom for Egypt to be itself, but with the possible implication that it will not be a great empire again and thus be either resource or threat to Judah (cf. Ezek 29:13–16).”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 532–534; Jer 46:25–26

### C-R9-20
**Claim:** Philistia 47:1–7: intro mentions Pharaoh striking Gaza, but poem has trouble from north—Nebuchadrezzar took Ashkelon year after Carchemish; Neco may have taken Gaza ~609 or after ~601 Egyptian repulse of Babylon. Gaza vulnerable as fought-over corridor; Judah brought trouble on itself. Poem: human-caused flood from north (vv. 2–4a) then Yahweh’s causation (4b–7). No rationale; not judgment for desert—wrong place, wrong time; Yahweh’s sovereignty even when reasons unknown. Not eschatological/apocalyptic. Protest to sword (v. 6) answered: Yahweh ordered it for Ashkelon and seacoast (v. 7).
**Quote:** “Jeremiah himself does not describe the attack on Philistia as an act of judgment or suggest that the Philistines have done anything to deserve what happens except be in the wrong place at the wrong time. It simply asserts once more that something that one might see as a random event within world history (like the events in Dan 11) is one in which Yahweh’s sovereignty is at work. … There seems no reason to see the poem as eschatological or apocalyptic. … It was Yahweh who gave the order for the slaughter, and it must continue until he says, ‘Enough.’”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 638–713; Jer 47:1–7
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R9-21
**Claim:** Moab 48 is most substantial OAN collection until Babylon 50–51; fits Moab’s First Testament prominence. Theme: Yahweh brings calamity, closes with restoration. No dates; may discourage Moabite-influenced worship (2 Kgs 23:13), anti-Babylon alliance (Jer 27:3), or assume Yahweh will act on Moab’s attacks (2 Kgs 24:2)—but length suggests more. Marks marked similarity to Isa 15–16, Isa 24, Num 21; Goldingay’s working hypothesis: Jeremiah using those in something like present form. Shared versions underscore Moab’s importance; territorial dispute north of Arnon underlies prominence.
**Quote:** “Until we come to Babylon in Jer 50–51, the Moab chapter is the most substantial collection of messages about another nation in Jeremiah. … Much of Jer 48 shows marked similarity to Moab material in Isaiah and Numbers…. I take this last, simplest possibility as my working hypothesis [Jeremiah using Isa 15–16; 24 and Num 21–24]. … Yahweh is promising to take back the land in the formerly Amorite territory north of Moab, which he claimed … and allocated to Reuben and Gad. … Yahweh does not take action against Moabite territory south of the Arnon, which he gave to Moab (Deut 2:9).”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 721–1100; Jer 48
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R9-23
**Claim:** Jer 48 is a collection (like Jer 2), not one battle narrative; transitions hard; prose footnotes; language Jeremianic. Main theme: Yahweh against Moab, devastating effect; sympathy often ironic underlining catastrophe; real divine grief possible as for Judah; closes with reverse irony—restoration in same terms as Judah’s. Judahite celebration of comeuppance must yield to celebration of restoration.
**Quote:** “The chapter’s main theme is an affirmation that Yahweh will act against Moab and that the effect on Moab will be devastating. It manifests considerable sympathy toward Moab in this connection, but the expressions of sympathy seem ironic; they are a way of underlining the depth of the catastrophe. No doubt Yahweh really does grieve at the need to bring such calamity to Moab, as he grieves at the need to bring calamity to Judah. And the chapter does close with a reverse irony: Yahweh promises Moab’s restoration in the same terms as he promises Judah’s restoration. Any Judahite celebration of Moab’s comeuppance must give way finally to celebration of its restoration.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 1110–1113; Jer 48
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R9-24
**Claim:** 48:1–10: imaginary lament; northern towns (Nebo, Kiriathaim, Heshbon, Madmen) destroyed—north of Arnon is Yahweh’s claimed land (Moses surveyed from Nebo). South (Horonaim, Luhith) reacts with outcry. First rationale: Moab relied on what it made and stores—divine images/shrine accoutrements; Chemosh goes to exile with priests/officials (cf. Amos 1:15). Destroyer to every town; curse on those who do Yahweh’s work treacherously / hold back sword from blood—agents must finish destruction thoroughly (work alien to Yahweh, Isa 28:21; Lam 3:33).
**Quote:** “For the first time, a reason is given for the dire fate that is coming on Moab. Relying on the wrong thing is an important theme in Jeremiah. … Mistaken reliance is key to life and death for other peoples, not just for Israel. Moab’s false reliance is the same as Judah’s. … As the Mesha inscription presupposes, Chemosh is Moab’s deity as Yahweh is Israel’s. But Chemosh does not have the power to save his people; rather, he and his ministers inevitably share their fate. … It may presuppose that Yahweh doesn’t enjoy commissioning such work; it is alien to him (Isa 28:21), and it doesn’t come from his heart (Lam 3:33).”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 1248–1256; Jer 48:1–10

Insofar as there is a basis for Yahweh’s action in Jer 49, it is simply Edom’s self-confidence. This difference suggests that Jer 49 might come from before 587 whereas Obadiah comes from after 587. ### C-R9-40
**Claim (synthesis — MT/LXX placement and internal order):** (1) Block placement: MT end vs LXX after 25—both sensible curator strategies. (2) Internal order: MT geographically/theologically ordered (Egypt→Philistia→eastern neighbors→distant→Babylon last); LXX more random with Babylon mid-sequence. (3) Unit-level: LXX shorter often (lacks Egypt 46:26b details; Moab 45–47; Ammon 6; variants on Edom/Damascus/Kedar/Elam); different editions reorder Ammon/Edom/Damascus/Kedar. (4) Elam in LXX as 25:14–19 (slice header: OAN as LXX 26:1–31:44 for whole block).
**Quote:** “We do not know whether either order is more original or whether they represent ways in which different curators assembled Jeremianic material; either position makes sense.” / “LXX’s order looks random, whereas there is a broad geographical and theological logic about MT’s.”
